note.explanation: This chapter connects the different states and forms of matter with chemistry branches, mixtures, and solubility. Matter may be a solid, liquid, gas, plasma, liquid crystal, or supercritical fluid. Chemistry is divided into branches so different kinds of substances and problems can be studied systematically. Solutions and crystallization also help explain how substances dissolve and how they can be purified.
examples: A fluorescent tube contains plasma: an electric current ionizes the gas inside it.
Potassium nitrate crystals can be obtained by dissolving the salt in hot water and then cooling the solution.
note.checkAnswer: Plasma is formed when a gas is ionized.
note.simple: Matter can take different forms, and substances can be mixed, dissolved, or purified in different ways. Chemistry has branches to help us study these topics.
note.checkQuestion: How is plasma formed in a fluorescent tube?
note.title: States of Matter and Phase Changes
steps: Identify the substance or process in the question.
Connect it with the relevant state of matter, chemistry branch, or property.
For a solution or crystallization question, consider the solute, solvent, and temperature.
Give the reason as well as the conclusion when the question asks why or explain.
note.answer: Plasma is a gas in which some particles have become electrically charged.

mcqs.stem: Q1.1. Matter is present in neon signs in the state of:
rationales: A neon sign does not operate with matter in a supercritical state.
Correct: the electric discharge ionizes the gas in the sign, forming plasma.
The gas is changed into plasma when the electric discharge passes through it.
A liquid crystal is not the state present in a neon sign.

mcqs.stem: Q1.2. Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in:
rationales: Geochemistry studies chemical processes and materials of the Earth, not chiefly the environmental hazards of shopping bags.
Inorganic chemistry studies inorganic substances and their reactions.
Analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts.
Correct: environmental chemistry studies chemicals and their effects in the environment.
Starch is a naturally occurring polymer.
Correct: polystyrene is a synthetic, man-made polymer.
Proteins are naturally occurring polymers made by living organisms.
Cellulose is a naturally occurring polymer in plant cell walls.

mcqs.stem: Q1.4. The crystals of which substance has rhombic shape?
rationales: Brass is an alloy, not the substance with rhombic crystals asked for here.
Correct: sulphur forms rhombic crystals.
Graphite has a layered structure rather than rhombic crystals.
Bronze is an alloy and is not the answer.

options: Slaked lime used for white wash
mcqs.stem: Q1.5. Which liquid among the following is a colloidal solution?
rationales: Correct: milk is an emulsion, a type of colloid.
Slaked lime in water is not the colloidal liquid intended here.
Vinegar solution is a true solution because its particles are dissolved at molecular level.
AgCl does not form the colloidal solution intended by this question in water.

options: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
A solution of potassium nitrate in water
mcqs.stem: Q1.6. Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
rationales: A solution of calcium hydroxide is treated as a solution, which is uniform in composition.
A solution of potassium nitrate is homogeneous.
Hot chocolate may appear mixed, but concrete is the clearly heterogeneous mixture in this list.
Correct: concrete has visibly different components and is not uniform throughout.

mcqs.stem: Q1.7. A state of matter whose properties are between those of liquids and crystalline solids:
rationales: Correct: liquid crystals show properties between those of ordinary liquids and crystalline solids.
A supercritical fluid is formed above its critical temperature and pressure.
Plasma is an ionized gas.
Dark matter is not the state of matter described in the question.

mcqs.stem: Q1.8. When the tiny visible particles of a substance are dispersed through a medium, the mixture is named as:
rationales: Particles in a true solution are too small to be seen as visible particles.
Correct: a colloid has dispersed particles in a medium that may be visible as a beam-scattering effect or under suitable observation.
Suspension particles are larger and can settle on standing.
Saturated describes the maximum amount of solute dissolved at a given condition, not this type of dispersed mixture.

options: The solubility will remain the same
The solubility will first increase with temperature and then it will decrease
mcqs.stem: Q1.9. A solution of KClO₃ has a solubility of about 13.2g per 100 cm³ at 40°C. How its solubility will be affected, if you decrease the temperature?
rationales: For this solid solute, lowering the temperature does not increase its solubility.
Correct: the solubility of KClO₃ decreases when the temperature is decreased.
The solubility of this solid changes with temperature.
This option does not describe the expected effect of decreasing the temperature.

mcqs.stem: Q1.10. You are studying the rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature. In which branch of chemistry this topic will fall?
rationales: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, but the question focuses on reaction rate and temperature.
Analytical chemistry concerns identification and measurement of substances.
Biochemistry concerns chemical processes in living organisms, but the stated focus is reaction rate under different temperatures.
Correct: physical chemistry studies rates of reactions and the effects of conditions such as temperature.

written.text: Q1.1. Why is there a need to divide Chemistry into many branches? Give three reasons.
written.finalAnswer: Chemistry is divided into branches because its knowledge is vast, specialization is needed, and different branches address different substances and applications.

rubric.why: Recognizes that chemistry covers a very large amount of knowledge.
rubric.description: State that chemistry is a vast subject.
rubric.how: Explain that the subject contains many topics and substances.

rubric.why: Shows why separate areas of study are useful.
rubric.description: Mention specialization.
rubric.how: Explain that people can study a particular area in depth.

rubric.why: Identifies the organized division of the subject.
rubric.description: Explain that branches organize different topics and problems.
rubric.how: Give an idea such as studying different substances or applications separately.

rubric.why: Completes the reasons with the practical value of the branches.
rubric.description: Refer to different applications or problems addressed by chemistry.
rubric.how: Link branches to the different kinds of work chemistry must do.

modelAnswer: Chemistry is a vast subject with a very large amount of knowledge.
Its division into branches allows specialization and systematic study.
Different branches deal with different substances, problems, and applications.
Therefore, chemistry is divided into many branches.

written.text: Q1.2. Reactions may take place due to electrons present outside the nucleus or they may take place inside the nucleus. Which branches of Chemistry cover these two types of reactions?
written.finalAnswer: Chemical reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are studied in chemistry; reactions inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.

rubric.why: Identifies the branch dealing with reactions involving extranuclear electrons.
rubric.description: Name chemistry for reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus.
rubric.how: State that these are ordinary chemical reactions.

rubric.why: Identifies the branch concerned with reactions inside the nucleus.
rubric.description: Name nuclear chemistry.
rubric.how: Match nuclear reactions with nuclear chemistry.

modelAnswer: Reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus are chemical reactions.
They are studied in chemistry.
Reactions taking place inside the nucleus are studied in nuclear chemistry.

written.text: Q1.3. What types of problems are solved in analytical chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: Analytical chemistry identifies the substances present in a sample and determines their amounts.

rubric.why: Identification is one of the two main kinds of analytical problem.
rubric.description: State that analytical chemistry identifies substances.
rubric.how: Mention finding what is present in a sample.

rubric.why: Quantitative analysis determines how much of a substance is present.
rubric.description: State that analytical chemistry measures amount.
rubric.how: Mention measuring the quantity or concentration in the sample.

modelAnswer: Analytical chemistry identifies the substances present in a sample.
It also determines the amount or concentration of each substance.

written.text: Q1.4. Both graphite and graphene have hexagonal layered structures. What is the difference?
written.finalAnswer: Graphite consists of many layers of carbon atoms, while graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.

rubric.why: Identifies graphite as a stack of carbon layers.
rubric.description: Describe graphite as many layers.
rubric.how: State that graphite has layers stacked together.

rubric.why: Identifies graphene as one atomic layer.
rubric.description: Describe graphene as one layer of carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Mention its single hexagonal carbon sheet.

modelAnswer: Graphite is made of many layers of carbon atoms arranged in hexagons.
Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.

written.text: Q1.5. Why are supercritical fluids important?
written.finalAnswer: Supercritical fluids are important because they combine useful properties of liquids and gases and can act as effective solvents for extraction and other processes.

rubric.why: Recognizes the mixed useful properties of the supercritical state.
rubric.description: State that supercritical fluids have properties of both liquids and gases.
rubric.how: Mention both kinds of properties.

rubric.why: Gives a practical use of supercritical fluids.
rubric.description: Mention their use as solvents or in extraction.
rubric.how: Give a suitable application.

modelAnswer: Supercritical fluids have useful properties of both liquids and gases.
They can act as effective solvents and are useful in extraction and other processes.

written.text: Q1.6. In which state does matter exist in the Sun?
written.finalAnswer: Plasma.

rubric.why: Names the state of matter present in the Sun.
rubric.description: Give the correct state.
rubric.how: Answer plasma.

modelAnswer: Matter in the Sun exists in the plasma state.

written.text: Q1.7. What is the importance of graphene?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene is important because it is extremely strong, light, thin, and conducts electricity very well, making it useful in electronics and other technologies.

rubric.why: Names an important property that makes graphene useful in electronic devices.
rubric.description: Mention its excellent electrical conductivity or electronic use.
rubric.how: Connect its conductivity to electronics.

rubric.why: Adds another important property supporting its wide use.
rubric.description: Mention a useful physical property.
rubric.how: Give at least one property such as strength, low mass, thinness, or flexibility.

modelAnswer: Graphene is extremely strong, light, and thin, and it conducts electricity very well.
These properties make it useful in electronics and other technologies.

written.text: Q1.8. Which form of matter do most of the material things in this world belong to?
written.finalAnswer: Most material things in the world belong to the solid state.

rubric.why: Names the state asked for.
rubric.description: State that most material things are solids.
rubric.how: Answer solid state.

modelAnswer: Most of the material things in this world belong to the solid state.

written.text: Q1.1. How does a supercritical state look like?
written.finalAnswer: A supercritical state has no distinct boundary between liquid and gas; it is a single fluid with liquid-like density and gas-like ability to flow and diffuse.

rubric.why: Describes the lack of a separate liquid-gas boundary.
rubric.description: State that there is no distinct boundary between liquid and gas.
rubric.how: Explain that the two phases are no longer visibly separate.

rubric.why: Identifies the material as one supercritical fluid phase.
rubric.description: Name it as a single fluid state.
rubric.how: Describe the appearance as one uniform fluid.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic liquid-like property.
rubric.description: Mention liquid-like density.
rubric.how: State that it can have density similar to a liquid.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic gas-like property.
rubric.description: Mention gas-like flow or diffusion.
rubric.how: State that it spreads or diffuses like a gas.

modelAnswer: In the supercritical state, there is no distinct boundary between the liquid and gas.
The substance is a single fluid.
It can have liquid-like density.
It can also flow and diffuse in a gas-like way.

written.text: Q1.2. In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?
written.finalAnswer: An electric discharge passes through the gas in the fluorescent tube and ionizes some of its atoms, producing plasma.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy source that acts on the gas.
rubric.description: Mention an electric discharge or current.
rubric.how: State that electricity passes through the tube.

rubric.why: Identifies the material in the tube that is changed.
rubric.description: Mention the gas in the tube.
rubric.how: Explain that the discharge acts on this gas.

rubric.why: Describes the change that produces charged particles.
rubric.description: State that the gas becomes ionized.
rubric.how: Mention that atoms lose or gain electrons and become charged.

rubric.why: Names the resulting state of matter.
rubric.description: Identify the product as plasma.
rubric.how: End by stating that ionized gas is plasma.

modelAnswer: An electric discharge passes through the gas in a fluorescent tube.
The discharge ionizes some of the gas atoms.
Charged particles are produced.
The ionized gas is plasma.

written.text: Q1.3. Most of the molecules we study in biochemistry are organic in nature. Where does the difference exist in organic and biochemistry branches of Chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, whereas biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes of living organisms, including their organic molecules.

rubric.why: Defines the principal subject of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: State that organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Name carbon compounds as its subject.

rubric.why: Defines the subject matter of biochemistry.
rubric.description: Link biochemistry with living organisms.
rubric.how: Mention their substances or processes.

rubric.why: Clarifies the chemical aspect of biochemistry.
rubric.description: Mention chemical processes or substances in living things.
rubric.how: Explain what is studied within living organisms.

rubric.why: Makes clear that subject area, not simply the presence of organic molecules, separates the branches.
rubric.description: Contrast the focus of the two branches.
rubric.how: State that biochemistry is defined by its focus on living systems.

modelAnswer: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
Biochemistry studies the chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
Biochemistry includes many organic molecules, but its special focus is living systems.

written.text: Q1.4. Give the reason of brilliance shown by diamond. Can you improve it?
written.finalAnswer: Diamond is brilliant because its high refractive index causes repeated total internal reflection of light inside it. Its brilliance can be improved by cutting and polishing it properly.

rubric.why: Gives the optical property responsible for diamond's brilliance.
rubric.description: Mention diamond's high refractive index.
rubric.how: Link the index to the bending and trapping of light.

rubric.why: Explains how light is reflected inside the diamond.
rubric.description: Mention internal reflection of light.
rubric.how: Explain that light is reflected repeatedly within the stone.

rubric.why: Identifies a way to increase brilliance.
rubric.description: Mention suitable cutting.
rubric.how: State that the diamond should be cut appropriately.

rubric.why: Completes the improvement method.
rubric.description: Mention polishing the diamond.
rubric.how: State that proper polishing improves its appearance.

modelAnswer: Diamond has a high refractive index.
Light is reflected repeatedly inside it, producing brilliance.
Its brilliance can be improved by suitable cutting.
Proper polishing also improves its brilliance.

written.text: Q1.5. Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.
written.finalAnswer: Water molecules attract the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in sodium chloride. The ions separate from the crystal, become surrounded by water molecules, and disperse through the water.

rubric.why: Identifies the positive ions in the ionic solid.
rubric.description: Name the sodium ions.
rubric.how: Write Na⁺ or sodium ions.

rubric.why: Identifies the negative ions in the ionic solid.
rubric.description: Name the chloride ions.
rubric.how: Write Cl⁻ or chloride ions.

rubric.why: Explains the interaction that separates and hydrates the ions.
rubric.description: Describe water molecules attracting or surrounding the ions.
rubric.how: Mention the attraction between polar water molecules and ions.

rubric.why: Describes the final result of dissolution.
rubric.description: State that the separated ions disperse in water.
rubric.how: Conclude that an aqueous solution forms.

modelAnswer: Sodium chloride consists of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions held together in a crystal.
Water molecules attract the oppositely charged ions.
The ions separate from the crystal and become surrounded by water molecules.
The hydrated ions disperse throughout the water to form a solution.

written.text: Q1.6. Why do different compounds have different solubilities in water at a particular temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Different compounds have different solubilities because their particles interact with water to different extents, depending on the nature of the solute and the attractions holding its particles together.

rubric.why: Recognizes that compounds have different chemical properties.
rubric.description: Refer to the different nature of the solutes.
rubric.how: State that each compound interacts differently.

rubric.why: Connects solubility to solute-water interactions.
rubric.description: Mention interactions or attractions between solute and water.
rubric.how: Explain that dissolving depends on attraction to water molecules.

rubric.why: Recognizes that the attractions within the compound also affect dissolution.
rubric.description: Mention the forces holding solute particles together.
rubric.how: Explain that these forces must be overcome for dissolution.

rubric.why: Links these interactions to the amount that dissolves.
rubric.description: Conclude that different balance of attractions gives different solubilities.
rubric.how: State that this is why the solubilities differ at the same temperature.

modelAnswer: Different compounds have different attractions between their particles.
They also interact with water molecules to different extents.
These attractions determine how readily their particles separate and mix with water.
Therefore, different compounds have different solubilities at the same temperature.

written.text: Q1.7. Why NaCl can not be crystallized from water just like KNO₃?
written.finalAnswer: The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature, unlike KNO₃. Cooling a hot saturated NaCl solution therefore does not make enough NaCl crystallize out in the same way.

rubric.why: Identifies the relevant property of NaCl.
rubric.description: Refer to NaCl solubility.
rubric.how: Compare how NaCl solubility changes with temperature.

rubric.why: States that NaCl solubility changes only a little with temperature.
rubric.description: Describe the small temperature effect.
rubric.how: Say that its solubility increases only slightly on heating.

rubric.why: Provides the required comparison substance.
rubric.description: Contrast NaCl with KNO₃.
rubric.how: State that KNO₃ solubility changes much more with temperature.

rubric.why: Connects the solubility difference to the crystallization result.
rubric.description: Explain why cooling does not yield NaCl crystals in the same way.
rubric.how: State that too little NaCl comes out of solution on cooling.

modelAnswer: The solubility of NaCl changes very little with temperature.
The solubility of KNO₃ increases much more when the water is heated.
On cooling, much more KNO₃ separates from its solution as crystals.
Cooling a saturated NaCl solution does not crystallize NaCl in the same way.

written.text: Q1.8. Why graphite is slippery to touch? Which property of graphite enables it to be used as lubricant?
written.finalAnswer: Graphite is slippery because its layers can slide over one another easily. This easy sliding of layers, due to weak forces between them, enables graphite to be used as a lubricant.

rubric.why: Recognizes graphite's layered structure.
rubric.description: Mention that graphite has layers.
rubric.how: State that its carbon atoms form layers.

rubric.why: Explains the immediate cause of slipperiness.
rubric.description: State that the layers slide over each other.
rubric.how: Explain that the layers move easily.

rubric.why: Explains why the layers can slide.
rubric.description: Mention weak forces between the layers.
rubric.how: Relate weak interlayer attraction to easy sliding.

rubric.why: Names the property or use asked for.
rubric.description: Connect easy layer-sliding with its use as a lubricant.
rubric.how: State that this property enables lubrication.

modelAnswer: Graphite consists of layers of carbon atoms.
The forces between the layers are weak.
The layers can slide over one another easily, so graphite feels slippery.
This easy sliding property enables graphite to be used as a lubricant.

written.text: Q1.1(a). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Rate of a reaction.
written.finalAnswer: Physical chemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly classifies reaction rate as a physical chemistry topic.
rubric.description: Name physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Give the branch that studies reaction rates.

modelAnswer: The rate of a reaction is studied in physical chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(b). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Digestion of food in human body.
written.finalAnswer: Biochemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly classifies a chemical process in the human body.
rubric.description: Name biochemistry.
rubric.how: Connect digestion with chemical processes in living organisms.

modelAnswer: Digestion of food in the human body is studied in biochemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(c). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Properties of plasma.
written.finalAnswer: Physical chemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly assigns the properties of a state of matter to physical chemistry.
rubric.description: Name physical chemistry.
rubric.how: Give the branch studying physical states and their properties.

modelAnswer: The properties of plasma are studied in physical chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(d). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Ecosystem.
written.finalAnswer: Environmental chemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly classifies the study of an ecosystem in environmental chemistry.
rubric.description: Name environmental chemistry.
rubric.how: Link an ecosystem with the environment.

modelAnswer: An ecosystem is studied in environmental chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(e). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Reactions taking place during fireworks.
written.finalAnswer: Inorganic chemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly assigns the fireworks reactions to the branch used for inorganic substances and their reactions.
rubric.description: Name inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: Give the branch for the reactions described in the textbook topic.

modelAnswer: Reactions taking place during fireworks are studied in inorganic chemistry.

written.text: Q1.1(f). Mention the name of the branch of Chemistry in which you will study this topic: Measurement of the absorption of wavelength with the help of ultraviolet spectrometer.
written.finalAnswer: Analytical chemistry.

rubric.why: Correctly identifies spectrometric measurement as analytical chemistry.
rubric.description: Name analytical chemistry.
rubric.how: Link measurement and analysis with analytical chemistry.

modelAnswer: Measurement of wavelength absorption with an ultraviolet spectrometer is studied in analytical chemistry.

written.text: Q1.2. What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
written.finalAnswer: Allotropes are different forms of the same element in the same physical state. Carbon occurs as diamond, graphite, graphene, and other forms; sulphur occurs mainly as rhombic, monoclinic, and plastic forms. Coal is an impure, largely amorphous form of carbon, whereas diamond is a crystalline form of pure carbon.

rubric.why: Defines allotropy.
rubric.description: Define allotropic forms as different forms of the same element.
rubric.how: Mention one element and its different forms.

rubric.why: Gives valid carbon allotropes.
rubric.description: Name carbon allotropes.
rubric.how: Give at least two correct forms.

rubric.why: Gives sulphur allotropes.
rubric.description: Name sulphur forms.
rubric.how: Give correct crystalline or plastic forms.

rubric.why: Describes coal appropriately in the comparison.
rubric.description: State that coal is impure and largely amorphous carbon.
rubric.how: Contrast its composition or structure with diamond.

rubric.why: Completes the comparison with diamond.
rubric.description: Describe diamond as crystalline pure carbon.
rubric.how: State its structure or purity.

modelAnswer: Allotropic forms are different forms of the same element in the same physical state.
Carbon has allotropes including diamond, graphite, and graphene.
Sulphur has rhombic, monoclinic, and plastic forms.
Coal is an impure, largely amorphous form of carbon.
Diamond is a crystalline form of pure carbon.

written.text: Q1.3. What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?
written.finalAnswer: A supercritical fluid is a substance above its critical temperature and pressure, where liquid and gas are no longer distinct phases. Unlike an ordinary liquid, it has no separate liquid-gas boundary and can spread and diffuse like a gas while retaining liquid-like density.

rubric.why: Identifies the conditions for the supercritical state.
rubric.description: Mention conditions above the critical point.
rubric.how: Refer to critical temperature and pressure.

rubric.why: States that liquid and gas are not distinct in the supercritical state.
rubric.description: Explain the absence of a separate liquid-gas phase boundary.
rubric.how: State that it exists as one fluid phase.

rubric.why: Gives a contrast in density with gas-like behaviour.
rubric.description: Mention liquid-like density.
rubric.how: State that it can retain high, liquid-like density.

rubric.why: Explains a way it differs from an ordinary liquid.
rubric.description: Mention gas-like spreading or diffusion.
rubric.how: Contrast its ability to diffuse with an ordinary liquid.

modelAnswer: A supercritical fluid exists above the critical temperature and pressure of a substance.
There is no distinct boundary between its liquid and gas phases.
It can have liquid-like density.
Unlike an ordinary liquid, it can spread and diffuse in a gas-like way.

written.text: Q1.4. Define solubility of a solute. How does the solubility of solutes change with the increase in temperature?
written.finalAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution. The solubility of most solid solutes increases with temperature, while the solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases.

rubric.why: Includes the limiting amount in the definition.
rubric.description: Define solubility using the maximum amount of solute.
rubric.how: State that the amount is the maximum that dissolves.

rubric.why: Shows the solution has reached the saturation limit.
rubric.description: Mention formation of a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Include saturation in the definition.

rubric.why: States the general temperature effect for solid solutes.
rubric.description: Say that most solids become more soluble as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Mention the usual increase for solid solutes.

rubric.why: Adds the contrasting behaviour of gases.
rubric.description: State that gas solubility usually decreases as temperature rises.
rubric.how: Mention the general trend for gases in liquids.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.
The solubility of most solid solutes increases as temperature increases.
The solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.

written.text: Q1.5. What types of movements are present in gaseous and liquid molecules?
written.finalAnswer: Gas molecules have translational, rotational, and vibrational movements. Liquid molecules also vibrate and rotate and can move translationally, but their movement is more restricted than that of gas molecules.

rubric.why: Names a principal molecular movement.
rubric.description: Mention translational movement.
rubric.how: State that molecules move from place to place.

rubric.why: Names another molecular movement.
rubric.description: Mention rotational movement.
rubric.how: State that molecules rotate.

rubric.why: Names the third molecular movement.
rubric.description: Mention vibrational movement.
rubric.how: State that molecules vibrate.

rubric.why: Distinguishes liquid molecular movement from the freer movement of gas molecules.
rubric.description: Describe the more restricted movement in liquids.
rubric.how: Mention that liquid molecules remain close and move past one another.

modelAnswer: Gas molecules have translational, rotational, and vibrational movements.
Liquid molecules also have vibrational and rotational movements.
They can move from place to place by sliding past one another.
Their translational movement is more restricted than that of gas molecules.

written.text: Q1.6. Differentiate between the areas which are studied under inorganic and organic chemistry.
written.finalAnswer: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, particularly hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

rubric.why: Describes the main scope of inorganic chemistry.
rubric.description: State what inorganic chemistry studies.
rubric.how: Mention elements and their compounds.

rubric.why: Clarifies the usual distinction involving carbon compounds.
rubric.description: Mention that most carbon compounds are excluded from inorganic chemistry.
rubric.how: State the usual exception for carbon compounds.

rubric.why: Describes the main scope of organic chemistry.
rubric.description: State that organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
rubric.how: Name carbon compounds as its focus.

rubric.why: Adds a suitable detail to the organic chemistry scope.
rubric.description: Mention hydrocarbons or their derivatives.
rubric.how: Give examples of the carbon compounds studied.

modelAnswer: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.
Its areas include hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

written.text: Q1.1. Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
written.finalAnswer: Dissolve impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water to make a saturated solution. Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities, then cool it so potassium nitrate crystals form. Filter and dry the crystals; soluble impurities remain in the mother liquor.

rubric.why: Uses the temperature-dependent solubility of potassium nitrate to prepare a concentrated solution.
rubric.description: Dissolve the impure salt in a small amount of hot water.
rubric.how: State that hot water is used to form a saturated or concentrated solution.

rubric.why: Removes insoluble impurities before crystals form.
rubric.description: Filter the hot solution.
rubric.how: Mention removal of insoluble solid impurities.

rubric.why: Cooling lowers potassium nitrate solubility and causes crystallization.
rubric.description: Cool the filtered solution.
rubric.how: Explain that crystals form as the solution cools.

rubric.why: Identifies the purified product recovered.
rubric.description: State that potassium nitrate crystals form.
rubric.how: Name the crystals collected.

rubric.why: Completes the purification by separating and preparing the crystals.
rubric.description: Collect and dry the crystals.
rubric.how: Filter off the crystals and dry them.

modelAnswer: Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water to prepare a saturated solution.
Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities.
Allow the clear filtrate to cool.
Potassium nitrate crystallizes as its solubility decreases on cooling.
Filter off the crystals and dry them; soluble impurities remain in the mother liquor.

written.text: Q1.2. Graphene is called a miracle material and it is the material of the future. Which of its many properties makes it very useful in electronics?
written.finalAnswer: Graphene's very high electrical conductivity and high electron mobility make it very useful in electronics.

Short questions usually earn marks for a precise definition, name, or two clear points; answer directly before adding explanation.
Constructed-response questions often ask for a cause-and-effect explanation. Link the structure or interaction to the observed property.
For descriptive comparisons, present both sides clearly, such as graphite versus graphene or organic versus inorganic chemistry.
For crystallization, marks are commonly earned for hot solvent, filtration, cooling, crystal collection, and drying in the correct order.
Use correct terms such as ionized gas, saturated solution, solubility, and allotrope.

yourTurn.question: Q1.1. Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
solution: Dissolve impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water to make a saturated solution.
Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities.
Potassium nitrate crystals form as the solution cools.
Filter off and dry the crystals; soluble impurities remain in the mother liquor.
yourTurn.answer: Purified potassium nitrate crystals are obtained by dissolving the impure salt in hot water, filtering, cooling, and collecting and drying the crystals.

hints: What kind of particles are in a gas after ionization?
The electric discharge removes electrons from some gas atoms, making charged particles.
yourTurn.question: Q1.2. In what way is plasma created in a fluorescent tube?
solution: An electric discharge passes through the gas in the fluorescent tube.
The discharge ionizes some of the gas atoms.
yourTurn.answer: An electric discharge ionizes the gas in the fluorescent tube, producing plasma.

example.question: Q1.5. Explain the dissolution of sodium chloride in water.
example.answer: Water molecules attract the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in sodium chloride. The ions separate from the crystal, become surrounded by water molecules, and disperse through the water.

explain.title: Chemistry has different branches
explain.body: Chemistry covers many substances, reactions, and applications. Branches make this large subject easier to organize and allow detailed study. For example, biochemistry deals with chemical processes in living things, while analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts.

explain.title: Matter has several states
explain.body: Solids, liquids, and gases are familiar states. Plasma is an ionized gas, liquid crystals have properties between liquids and crystalline solids, and supercritical fluids form above a substance's critical temperature and pressure.

explain.title: Structure affects properties
explain.body: Carbon forms different allotropes. Graphite contains layers that slide over one another, so it is slippery; graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern. Sulphur also has different forms, including rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.

explain.title: Solutions and solubility
explain.body: A solute dissolves in a solvent to form a solution. Different solutes have different solubilities because they interact differently with the solvent. For most solids, solubility increases as temperature rises; gases dissolved in liquids generally become less soluble as temperature rises.

explain.title: Crystallization purifies a substance
explain.body: Dissolve a soluble solid in hot water, remove insoluble impurities by filtration, and cool the clear solution. As solubility falls, crystals form. Collect and dry the crystals; many soluble impurities stay in the remaining solution.

mistakes: Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: plasma contains charged particles because the gas has been ionized.
Do not describe graphene as many layers; graphene is one layer, while graphite has many layers.
Do not confuse analytical chemistry, which identifies and measures substances, with physical chemistry, which studies properties and reaction rates.
When explaining dissolution, include both the separation of ions and their interaction with water molecules.
Do not say that all solubilities change in the same direction with temperature; most solid solutes and gases behave differently.
For crystallization, do not cool the solution before removing insoluble impurities, and do not forget to collect and dry the crystals.
Do not call coal a pure crystalline form of carbon; distinguish it from diamond.
